     3	## Source
     4	https://ourworldindata.org/vaccination
     5	
     6	## History of Vaccine Development
     7	
     8	The first vaccine was created by Edward Jenner in 1796 against smallpox, using cowpox to trigger immunity. It took nearly a century before the next vaccine (rabies) was developed, because scientists didn't yet understand germ theory. Once Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch established germ theory in the late 19th century, vaccines for rabies, cholera, and anthrax followed.
     9	
    10	The timeline from pathogen identification to vaccine licensure has shortened dramatically over the past 140 years:
    11	
    12	| Disease | Pathogen Identified | Vaccine Licensed | Gap (Years) |
    13	|---|---|---|---|
    14	| Typhoid fever | 1884 | 1989 | 105 |
    15	| Meningitis | 1889 | 1981 | 92 |
    16	| Whooping cough | 1906 | 1948 | 42 |
    17	| Polio | 1908 | 1955 | 47 |
    18	| Measles | 1953 | 1963 | 10 |
    19	| Chickenpox | 1953 | 1995 | 42 |
    20	| Hepatitis B | 1965 | 1981 | 16 |
    21	| Ebola | 1976 | 2019 | 43 |
    22	| COVID-19 | 2020 | 2020 | <1 |
    23	
    24	![Vaccination innovation timeline from 1880 to 2020](./assets/figure_3.jpg)
    25	
    26	Modern tools — advanced microscopy, genome sequencing, mRNA technology, and virus-like particles — have enabled faster and more precise vaccine design.
    27	
    28	## Dramatic Disease Reductions in the United States
    29	
    30	Data from Roush and Murphy (2007) shows the reduction in cases and deaths for vaccine-preventable diseases in the US after vaccine introduction. Several diseases achieved 100% elimination of both cases and deaths.
    31	
    32	| Disease | Pre-Vaccine Cases (per million/yr) | Post-Vaccine Cases (per million/yr) | Case Reduction | Pre-Vaccine Deaths (per million/yr) | Death Reduction |
    33	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
    34	| Diphtheria | 158 | 0 | 100% | 13.7 | 100% |
    35	| Measles | 3,044 | 0.2 | 99.99% | 2.5 | 100% |
    36	| Smallpox | 250 | 0 | 100% | 2.9 | 100% |
    37	| Acute polio | 141 | 0 | 100% | 10 | 100% |
    38	| Pertussis | 1,534 | 52 | 96.6% | 30.8 | 99.7% |
    39	| Rubella | 242 | 0.04 | 99.98% | 0.09 | 100% |
    40	| Hepatitis A | 465 | 51 | 89% | 0.5 | 88.7% |
    41	| Acute hepatitis B | 273 | 44 | 83.9% | 1 | 83.6% |
    42	| Pneumococcal | 233 | 139 | 40.5% | 24 | 31.3% |
    43	
    44	![US vaccine-preventable disease reductions](./assets/figure_1.jpg)
    45	
    46	## Measles Elimination Across US States
    47	
    48	A heatmap of measles cases per 100,000 across all 50 US states from 1929 to 2022 shows the dramatic impact of vaccination. Three key milestones transformed the landscape:
    49	
    50	- **1963**: First measles vaccine developed by John Enders
    51	- **1971**: MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccine developed by Maurice Hilleman
    52	- **1980**: Vaccination became mandatory for children entering kindergarten
    53	
    54	Before 1963, nearly every state experienced high measles incidence (100–1,000+ cases per 100,000). After the 1980 mandate, cases dropped to near zero across all states, with only sporadic outbreaks.
    55	
    56	![Measles heatmap across US states](./assets/figure_2.jpg)
    57	
    58	## Smallpox Eradication: The Greatest Vaccination Success
    59	
    60	Smallpox was declared eradicated worldwide in 1980 — the only human disease to be fully eliminated through vaccination. Key factors enabling eradication: the virus infected only humans, symptoms were distinguishable, and the vaccine was cheap and effective. The WHO passed a resolution to eradicate smallpox in 1959, launched an intensified campaign in 1967, and the last natural case occurred in Somalia in 1977.
    61	
    62	## Herd Immunity and Remaining Challenges
    63	
    64	Vaccines protect not only individuals but entire communities through herd immunity. When enough people are vaccinated, pathogens cannot spread effectively, shielding those who cannot be vaccinated — newborns, immunocompromised individuals, and cancer patients on chemotherapy.
    65	
    66	However, significant challenges remain. Pneumococcal disease has seen only a 40.5% reduction in cases and 31.3% in deaths. Hepatitis A and B still show incomplete control. Globally, not everyone has access to vaccines, supply shortages put children at risk, and poor scientific understanding can reduce trust and uptake.
    67	
    68	## Key Findings
    69	
    70	- **Vaccines achieved 100% elimination** of cases and deaths for diphtheria, smallpox, and both forms of polio in the US.
    71	- **Vaccine development timelines have collapsed** from over 100 years (typhoid) to under 1 year (COVID-19), driven by mRNA technology and genomic tools.
    72	- **Measles cases dropped to near zero** across all 50 US states following the 1980 kindergarten vaccination mandate.
    73	- **Smallpox remains the only human disease eradicated** through vaccination, certified in 1980 after a global campaign.
    74	- **Gaps persist** for pneumococcal disease (40.5% case reduction), hepatitis A (89%), and hepatitis B (83.9%), highlighting the need for improved access, coverage, and newer vaccines.

    10	
    11	## When to Use
    12	
    13	Use when the main artifact is a Microsoft PowerPoint presentation or `.pptx` deck, especially when layouts, templates, placeholders, notes, comments, charts, extraction, editing, or final visual quality matter.
    14	
    15	## Core Rules
    16	
    17	### 1. Choose the workflow before touching the deck
    18	
    19	- Reading text, editing an existing deck, rebuilding from a template, and creating from scratch are different jobs with different failure modes.
    20	- For text extraction or inspection, read the deck before editing it.
    21	- Text extraction plus thumbnail-style visual inspection is safer than editing from shape assumptions alone.
    22	- For template-driven work, inventory the deck before replacing content.
    23	- For deep edits, remember a `.pptx` file is OOXML with separate parts for slides, layouts, masters, media, notes, and comments.
    24	- If a template exists, template fidelity beats generic slide-design instincts.
    25	- Reusing or duplicating a good existing slide is often safer than rebuilding it and hoping the theme still matches.
    26	
    27	### 2. Inventory the deck before replacing content
    28	
    29	- Count the reusable layouts, real placeholders, notes, comments, media, and recurring typography or color patterns first.
    30	- Placeholder indexes and layout indexes are not portable assumptions.
    31	- Inspect the actual slide or template before targeting title, body, chart, or image shapes.
    32	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked assets can live outside the visible slide surface.
    33	- A missing or wrong placeholder target can silently land content in the wrong box or wrong layer.
    34	- Master and layout settings can override local slide edits, so the visible problem is not always on the slide you are editing.
    35	
    36	### 3. Match content to the actual placeholders
    37	
    38	- Count the actual content pieces before choosing a layout.
    39	- Pick layouts based on the real number of ideas, columns, images, or charts the slide needs.
    40	- Do not force two ideas into a three-column slide or cram dense text under a chart.
    41	- Category counts and data series lengths must match or charts will break in ugly ways.
    42	- Explicit sizing beats wishful thinking: text boxes, images, and charts need real space, not "it should fit".
    43	- Do not choose a layout with more placeholders than the content can meaningfully fill.
    44	- Quote layouts are for real quotes, and image-led layouts are for slides that actually have images.
    45	- For chart-, table-, or image-heavy slides, full-slide or two-column layouts are usually safer than stacking dense text above the visual.
    46	
    47	### 4. Preserve the deck's visual language
    48	
    49	- Theme, master, and layout files usually decide fonts, colors, and hierarchy more than any one slide does.
    50	- Start from the deck's actual theme, fonts, spacing, and aspect ratio instead of improvising a new style.
    51	- Reuse the deck's own alignment and spacing system instead of inventing a second visual language.
    52	- Use common fonts for portability and strong contrast for readability.
    53	- Preserve the template's visual logic first; originality matters less than not breaking the deck's existing language.
    54	- Combining slides from multiple sources requires normalizing themes, masters, and alignment afterward.
    55	
    56	### 5. Run content QA and visual QA separately
    57	
    58	- Text overflow, bad alignment, clipped shapes, weak contrast, and placeholder leftovers are normal first-pass failures.
    59	- Run both content QA and visual QA; missing text and broken layout are different failure classes.
    60	- Render or inspect the actual deck output before delivery when layout matters.
    61	- Search for leftover template junk, sample labels, and placeholder text before calling the deck finished.
    62	- Check notes, comments, labels, legends, and chart/table semantics separately from the visual pass.
    63	- A deck can pass text extraction and still fail on overlap, clipping, wrong theme inheritance, or broken notes.
    64	- Thumbnail grids and rendered slides usually reveal layout bugs faster than code or text inspection.
    65	- Assume the first render is wrong and do at least one fix-and-verify cycle before calling the deck finished.
    66	- Re-check affected slides after each fix because one spacing change often creates another issue.
    67	
    68	### 6. Keep decks portable and review-safe
    69	
    70	- Template masters can override direct edits in surprising ways.
    71	- Complex effects may degrade across PowerPoint, LibreOffice, and conversion pipelines, so keep important content robust without them.
    72	- Image sizing, font substitution, and placeholder mismatch are common reasons a deck looks good in code and bad on screen.
    73	- Notes, comments, linked media, and merged decks can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    74	
    75	## Common Traps
    76	
    77	- Placeholder text and sample charts often survive template reuse if not explicitly replaced.
    78	- Directly editing one slide can fail if the real issue lives in the master or layout.
    79	- Charts, icons, and text boxes need enough space; near-collisions are usually visible only after rendering.
    80	- Layout indexes vary by template, so built-in assumptions from one deck often break in another.
    81	- A missing placeholder or wrong shape target can silently put content in the wrong place.
    82	- Counting the text ideas after choosing the layout usually leads to empty placeholders, weak hierarchy, or leftover template junk.
    83	- Font substitution can move line breaks and wreck careful spacing.
    84	- Speaker notes, comments, and linked media can stay broken even when the visible slide looks fine.
    85	- A deck can pass text inspection and still fail visually because of overlap, contrast, or edge clipping.
    86	- Editing from one slide alone can miss the real source of truth in the theme, master, or layout definitions.
    87	- Choosing a quote, comparison, or multi-column layout without matching content usually makes the deck look templated rather than intentional.
    88	- Combining or duplicating slides without checking masters and themes can create subtle inconsistency slide by slide.
    89	- Aspect-ratio mismatches like `16:9` versus `4:3` can shift every placement decision even when each slide looks locally reasonable.
    90

from pptx import Presentation
from pptx.util import Inches, Pt
from pptx.dml.color import RgbColor
from pptx.enum.text import PP_ALIGN, MSO_ANCHOR
from pptx.enum.shapes import MSO_SHAPE
from pptx.oxml.ns import nsmap
from pptx.oxml import parse_xml
import os

# Create output directory
os.makedirs('/app/output', exist_ok=True)

# Create presentation 16:9
prs = Presentation()
prs.slide_width = Inches(13.333)
prs.slide_height = Inches(7.5)

# Define color palette - professional public health theme
DARK_BLUE = RgbColor(0x1A, 0x2E, 0x5A)      # Primary dark blue
TEAL = RgbColor(0x00, 0x8B, 0x8B)           # Accent teal
LIGHT_GRAY = RgbColor(0xF5, 0xF5, 0xF5)     # Background
WHITE = RgbColor(0xFF, 0xFF, 0xFF)
DARK_GRAY = RgbColor(0x33, 0x33, 0x33)
MEDIUM_GRAY = RgbColor(0x66, 0x66, 0x66)
RED_ACCENT = RgbColor(0xC0, 0x00, 0x00)     # For emphasis
GREEN_ACCENT = RgbColor(0x2E, 0x7D, 0x32)   # For positive data

def add_background(slide, color=WHITE):
    background = slide.shapes.add_shape(
        MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, 0, 0, prs.slide_width, prs.slide_height
    )
    background.fill.solid()
    background.fill.fore_color.rgb = color
    background.line.fill.background()
    # Send to back
    spTree = slide.shapes._spTree
    sp = background._element
    spTree.remove(sp)
    spTree.insert(2, sp)

def add_title_bar(slide, title_text, subtitle_text=None):
    # Title bar background
    bar = slide.shapes.add_shape(
        MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, 0, 0, prs.slide_width, Inches(1.3)
    )
    bar.fill.solid()
    bar.fill.fore_color.rgb = DARK_BLUE
    bar.line.fill.background()
    
    # Title text
    title_box = slide.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(0.5), Inches(0.25), Inches(12.3), Inches(0.6))
    tf = title_box.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = title_text
    p.font.size = Pt(28)
    p.font.bold = True
    p.font.color.rgb = WHITE
    p.font.name = "Calibri"
    
    if subtitle_text:
        p2 = tf.add_paragraph()
        p2.text = subtitle_text
        p2.font.size = Pt(14)
        p2.font.color.rgb = RgbColor(0xCC, 0xCC, 0xCC)
        p2.font.name = "Calibri"
        p2.space_before = Pt(4)

def add_footer(slide, text="Source: Our World in Data"):
    footer = slide.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(0.5), Inches(7.15), Inches(6), Inches(0.3))
    tf = footer.text_frame
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = text
    p.font.size = Pt(10)
    p.font.color.rgb = MEDIUM_GRAY
    p.font.name = "Calibri"
    p.font.italic = True

def add_slide_number(slide, num, total=8):
    box = slide.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(12.3), Inches(7.15), Inches(0.8), Inches(0.3))
    tf = box.text_frame
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = f"{num}/{total}"
    p.font.size = Pt(10)
    p.font.color.rgb = MEDIUM_GRAY
    p.font.name = "Calibri"
    p.alignment = PP_ALIGN.RIGHT

# ============================================
# SLIDE 1: Title Slide
# ============================================
slide_layout = prs.slide_layouts[6]  # Blank
slide1 = prs.slides.add_slide(slide_layout)
add_background(slide1, DARK_BLUE)

# Main title
title_box = slide1.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(0.8), Inches(2.2), Inches(11.7), Inches(1.5))
tf = title_box.text_frame
tf.word_wrap = True
p = tf.paragraphs[0]
p.text = "The Power of Vaccination: From Smallpox Eradication to COVID-19 in Record Time"
p.font.size = Pt(40)
p.font.bold = True
p.font.color.rgb = WHITE
p.font.name = "Calibri"
p.line_spacing = 1.2

# Subtitle
sub_box = slide1.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(0.8), Inches(3.9), Inches(11.7), Inches(0.6))
tf2 = sub_box.text_frame
p2 = tf2.paragraphs[0]
p2.text = "A data-driven overview of vaccine impact across two centuries (1796–2020)"
p2.font.size = Pt(20)
p2.font.color.rgb = RgbColor(0xAA, 0xCC, 0xCC)
p2.font.name = "Calibri"

# Source attribution
src_box = slide1.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(0.8), Inches(6.5), Inches(11.7), Inches(0.4))
tf3 = src_box.text_frame
p3 = tf3.paragraphs[0]
p3.text = "Source: Our World in Data | Audience: Public Health Professionals & Policy Analysts"
p3.font.size = Pt(12)
p3.font.color.rgb = RgbColor(0x88, 0x88, 0x88)
p3.font.name = "Calibri"
p3.font.italic = True

# Accent line
line = slide1.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, Inches(0.8), Inches(3.7), Inches(2), Inches(0.05))
line.fill.solid()
line.fill.fore_color.rgb = TEAL
line.line.fill.background()

# ============================================
# SLIDE 2: Vaccine Timeline Acceleration
# ============================================
slide2 = prs.slides.add_slide(slide_layout)
add_background(slide2, WHITE)
add_title_bar(slide2, "From 100 Years to Under 1 Year: Vaccine Development Is Accelerating")
add_footer(slide2)
add_slide_number(slide2, 2)

# Horizontal bar chart using shapes
chart_data = [
    ("Typhoid fever", 105),
    ("Meningitis", 92),
    ("Whooping cough", 42),
    ("Polio", 47),
    ("Measles", 10),
    ("Chickenpox", 42),
    ("Hepatitis B", 16),
    ("Ebola", 43),
    ("COVID-19", 0.5),
]

max_val = 105
chart_left = Inches(1.2)
chart_top = Inches(1.6)
chart_width = Inches(9.5)
chart_height = Inches(5.0)
bar_height = Inches(0.38)
row_spacing = Inches(0.52)

for i, (disease, years) in enumerate(chart_data):
    y = chart_top + i * row_spacing
    bar_width = (years / max_val) * chart_width
    
    # Label
    lbl = slide2.shapes.add_textbox(chart_left - Inches(1.1), y, Inches(1.05), bar_height)
    tf = lbl.text_frame
    tf.word_wrap = True
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = disease
    p.font.size = Pt(11)
    p.font.color.rgb = DARK_GRAY
    p.font.name = "Calibri"
    p.alignment = PP_ALIGN.RIGHT
    
    # Bar
    color = RED_ACCENT if disease == "COVID-19" else TEAL
    bar = slide2.shapes.add_shape(MSO_SHAPE.RECTANGLE, chart_left, y, bar_width, bar_height)
    bar.fill.solid()
    bar.fill.fore_color.rgb = color
    bar.line.fill.background()
    
    # Value label
    val = slide2.shapes.add_textbox(chart_left + bar_width + Inches(0.1), y, Inches(1.0), bar_height)
    tf = val.text_frame
    p = tf.paragraphs[0]
    p.text = f"{years} yr" if years >= 1 else "<1 yr"
    p.font.size = Pt(11)
    p.font.bold = True
    p.font.color.rgb = color
    p.font.name = "Calibri"

# Highlight annotation for COVID-19
ann_box = slide2.shapes.add_textbox(Inches(10.8), Inches(6.0), Inches(2.2), Inches(0.8))
tf = ann_box.text_frame
tf.word_wrap = True
p = tf.paragraphs[0]
p.text = "COVID-19: Record-breaking <1 year via mRNA technology"
p.font.size = Pt(11)
p.font.bold = True
p.font.color.rgb = RED_ACCENT
p.font.name = "Calibri"

# ============================================
# SLIDE 3: US Disease Elimination
# ============================================
slide3 = prs.slides.add_slide(slide_layout)
add_background(slide3, WHITE)
add_title_bar(slide3, "100% Case Reduction Achieved for Diphtheria, Polio, and Smallpox in the US")
add_footer(slide3, "Source: Roush & Murphy (2007), Our World in Data")
add_slide_number(slide3, 3)

# Table data
table_data = [
    ["Disease", "Pre-Vaccine Cases\n(per million/yr)", "Post-Vaccine Cases\n(per million/yr)", "Case Reduction", "Pre-Vaccine Deaths\n(per million/yr)", "Death Reduction"],
    ["Diphtheria", "158", "0", "100%", "13.7", "100%"],
    ["Smallpox", "250", "0", "100%", "2.9", "100%"],
    ["Acute polio", "141", "0", "100%", "10", "100%"],
